title: Subspaces, sums and direct sums
objectives: Prove a subset is a subspace, and tell a sum from a direct sum.

screens.title: The two axes together
screens.prose: Let $A = \{(x, y) : xy = 0\}$, the union of the two axes in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Every point of $A$ lies on one axis or the other. $\mathbf{u}$ slides along the $x$-axis and $\mathbf{w}$ along the $y$-axis.
screens.question: Drag $\mathbf{u}$ to $(3, 0)$ and $\mathbf{w}$ to $(0, 2)$.

hints.text: Each head can move only along its own axis.
$\mathbf{u}$ goes three units right; $\mathbf{w}$ two units up.
Put $\mathbf{u}$ at $(3, 0)$ and $\mathbf{w}$ at $(0, 2)$.

feedback.correct: Right. Both are in $A$, and their sum is $(3, 2)$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Move $\mathbf{u}$ to $x = 3$ and $\mathbf{w}$ to $y = 2$.

byKey.u: $\mathbf{u}$ is not at $(3, 0)$ yet. Slide it along the $x$-axis.
byKey.w: $\mathbf{w}$ is not at $(0, 2)$ yet. Slide it up the $y$-axis.

explain.text: Both vectors are in $A$. Their sum $(3, 2)$ has $xy = 6 \ne 0$, so it is not. $A$ loses sums.

screens.title: When does the sum stay?
screens.prose: Slide $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ anywhere on their axes, including back to the origin. The caption shows the sum and its product $xy$. The sum is in $A$ exactly when $xy = 0$.
screens.question: When is $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ in $A$?

options.text: Always, since $\mathbf{u}$ and $\mathbf{w}$ are both in $A$
options.why: You assumed sums stay. The caption shows $xy = 6$ for $(3, 2)$.
Slide $\mathbf{w}$ back to the origin: then the sum is $\mathbf{u}$, which is in $A$.

hints.text: Try $\mathbf{w}$ at the origin.
With both non-zero, the sum has two non-zero entries.
The sum stays only when one of them is $\mathbf{0}$.

feedback.correct: Right. Two non-zero vectors on different axes add to a point off both.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Watch the caption as one vector returns to the origin.

explain.text: $(a, 0) + (0, b) = (a, b)$, and $ab = 0$ only when $a = 0$ or $b = 0$. So $A$ holds $\mathbf{0}$ and all multiples, but not all sums. It fails to be a vector space.

screens.title: The subspace test
screens.prose: A subset $U$ of $V$ is a **subspace** when it is a vector space with $V$'s own operations. Axler 1.34: it is enough that $U$ contains $\mathbf{0}$, is closed under addition and is closed under scalar multiplication. $A$ fails the middle check.
screens.question: Why need we not check commutativity and the rest for $U$?

options.text: They hold for all vectors of $V$, so they hold in $U$, which uses $V$'s operations.
They always fail for subsets, so there is nothing to check.
options.why: You thought they fail. They hold in $V$, so they hold for every vector in $U$.
You leaned on $\mathbf{0}$ alone. Closure is needed too, or sums could leave $U$.

options.text: Only commutativity is free; the others must be checked.
options.why: You freed only one. Every identity that holds in $V$ holds in $U$.

hints.text: The operations on $U$ are those of $V$.
An equation true for every vector of $V$ is true for every vector of $U$.
Only the checks that say we stay inside $U$ are new.

feedback.correct: Right. $U$ borrows the operations, so it inherits every identity.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what is new about $U$ compared with $V$.

explain.text: Commutativity, associativity and distributivity are equations about vectors of $V$. They stay true in $U$. What can go wrong is leaving $U$, which the three checks rule out.

screens.title: A plane through the origin
screens.prose: Claim: $U = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 0\}$ is a subspace. The picture shows $U$ with two of its vectors and their sum. Rotate it to see the sum lie in the plane.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: If $\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y} \in U$, then $(x_1 + y_1) + 2(x_2 + y_2) + 3(x_3 + y_3)$ $= 0 + 0 = 0$, so $\mathbf{x} + \mathbf{y} \in U$.
If $\mathbf{x} \in U$ and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$, then $\lambda x_1 + 2\lambda x_2 + 3\lambda x_3$ $= \lambda \cdot 0 = 0$, so $\lambda\mathbf{x} \in U$.
$(1, 1, -1)$ and $(3, 0, -1)$ are in $U$, and so is their sum, so $U$ is closed under addition.
lines.why: You checked one pair. Closure must hold for every pair in $U$.

hints.text: The three checks may come in any order; the conclusion comes last.
Each check substitutes into $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3$.
Zero; sums; multiples; conclude.

feedback.correct: Right. Three checks, each from the defining equation, then the conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Give the three checks for arbitrary vectors, then conclude.

byKey.d1: You kept the line with two particular vectors. One pair passing proves nothing about the rest.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Each check puts a general vector into $x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3$. The right side 0 survives adding and scaling. With a right side of 4 it would not, as the quiz shows.

screens.title: Subspaces of functions
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^{[0,1]}$, $p$ and $q$ both have value 1 at 0, and $p + q$ has value 2 there. Sums and multiples of continuous functions are continuous; `analysis` l15-epsilon-delta proves it.
screens.question: Which are subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^{[0,1]}$? Select all that apply.

options.why: You ticked $f(0) = 1$. The picture shows $(p + q)(0) = 2$, and the zero function is missing.
You ticked non-negative functions. $-1$ times one is negative, so scaling leaves the set.

hints.text: Run the three checks on each set.
The zero function has $f(0) = 0$, not 1.
The first three pass; $f(0) = 1$ and $f \ge 0$ fail.

feedback.correct: Right. Three are subspaces; $f(0) = 1$ and $f \ge 0$ are not.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Test $\mathbf{0}$, a sum and $-1$ times a function in each set.

byKey.f1: You ticked $f(0) = 1$. A sum has value 2 at 0, as the dot at $(0, 2)$ shows.
byKey.pos: You ticked $f \ge 0$. Multiplying by $-1$ makes the values negative.

explain.text: Conditions such as $f(0) = 0$ or $f(0) = f(1)$ are equations with zero on one side, so they survive sums and multiples. $f(0) = 1$ does not even hold for the zero function. Continuity passes by the analysis result.

screens.title: The sum of two subspaces
screens.prose: The **sum** of subspaces is $U + W = \{\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w} : \mathbf{u} \in U, \mathbf{w} \in W\}$. Here $U$ is the $x_1$-axis and $W$ the $x_2$-axis in $\mathbb{R}^3$. The chained arrows show one sum $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$.
screens.question: What is $U + W$?

options.text: The plane $x_3 = 0$, the smallest subspace holding both axes

options.why: You took the union. It loses sums, as $A$ did, so it is not a subspace.
You went too far. Every $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ has third entry 0.
You kept only the intersection. The sum holds every $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$.

hints.text: Write a general $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$.
Every $(a, b, 0)$ appears: the plane $x_3 = 0$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Work out $(a, 0, 0) + (0, b, 0)$ for all $a$ and $b$.

explain.text: Every sum is $(a, b, 0)$, so $U + W$ is the plane $x_3 = 0$. Any subspace holding $U$ and $W$ holds all these sums. So $U + W$ is the smallest subspace containing both.

screens.title: When is a sum direct?
screens.prose: $U_1 + \dots + U_m$ is a **direct sum**, written $U_1 \oplus \dots \oplus U_m$, when each of its vectors is written in exactly one way. Axler 1.45: it is direct when $\mathbf{0}$ has only the representation with every piece $\mathbf{0}$. Prove that direction.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + \mathbf{u}_m$, with each $\mathbf{u}_k \in U_k$, forces every $\mathbf{u}_k = \mathbf{0}$.
Take $\mathbf{v}$ written two ways: $\mathbf{v} = \mathbf{u}_1 + \dots + \mathbf{u}_m$ $= \mathbf{w}_1 + \dots + \mathbf{w}_m$, with $\mathbf{u}_k, \mathbf{w}_k \in U_k$.
Each $\mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{w}_k$ is in $U_k$, because $U_k$ is a subspace.
So every $\mathbf{u}_k - \mathbf{w}_k = \mathbf{0}$ by line 1: the two ways are the same. $\blacksquare$

lines.why: You wrote $\mathbf{v}$ only once. Uniqueness needs two ways to compare.

hints.text: Uniqueness: take two representations of the same $\mathbf{v}$.
Subtract them to get a representation of $\mathbf{0}$.
Assume; two ways; subtract; pieces in $U_k$; all zero.

feedback.correct: Right. Subtracting two representations gives one of $\mathbf{0}$, which must be trivial.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $\mathbf{v}$ two ways and subtract.

byKey.x1: You wrote $\mathbf{v}$ in one way. To show two ways agree, you need both on the page.
byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: Two ways of writing $\mathbf{v}$ differ by a way of writing $\mathbf{0}$. Line 1 says that way is trivial, so the pieces agree. The other direction is quick: $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{0} + \dots + \mathbf{0}$ is already one way.

screens.title: Two subspaces
screens.prose: For two subspaces there is a simpler test. Axler 1.46: $U + W$ is direct exactly when $U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}$. Prove that an intersection of $\{\mathbf{0}\}$ makes the sum direct.
screens.question: Put the lines in order. One line does not belong: move it to Left out.

lines.text: Suppose $U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}$, and let $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ with $\mathbf{u} \in U$, $\mathbf{w} \in W$.
Then $\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{w}$, and $-\mathbf{w} \in W$, so $\mathbf{u} \in U \cap W$.
So $\mathbf{0}$ has only the trivial representation, and $U + W$ is direct by Axler 1.45. $\blacksquare$

hints.text: Use the lemma: look at a representation of $\mathbf{0}$.
From $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$, the vector $\mathbf{u}$ is also in $W$.
Assume; $\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{w} \in W$; both zero; direct.

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{u}$ lands in both subspaces, so it is $\mathbf{0}$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Start from $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ and show $\mathbf{u}$ is in $W$.

byKey.left-out: You left out a line the proof needs.

explain.text: $\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{w}$ puts $\mathbf{u}$ in $W$ as well as $U$. The only common vector is $\mathbf{0}$, so both pieces vanish. Conversely, a non-zero $\mathbf{v}$ in both gives $\mathbf{0} = \mathbf{v} + (-\mathbf{v})$, two ways.

screens.title: Three subspaces
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^3$ take $U_1 = \{(x, y, 0)\}$, a plane, and the lines $U_2 = \{(0, 0, z)\}$ and $U_3 = \{(0, y, y)\}$. Each pair meets only in $\mathbf{0}$. Rotate the picture to check.
screens.question: Is $U_1 + U_2 + U_3$ a direct sum?

options.text: Yes, since every pair meets only at $\mathbf{0}$
options.why: You used the two-subspace test on three. It does not extend: look for a non-trivial way to write $\mathbf{0}$.

options.text: Yes, since the sum is all of $\mathbb{R}^3$
options.why: Reaching $\mathbb{R}^3$ says nothing about uniqueness. Direct is about writing vectors in one way.

hints.text: Use the lemma: can $\mathbf{0}$ be written with non-zero pieces?
Start with $(0, 1, 0) \in U_1$ and $(0, 0, 1) \in U_2$, as drawn.
Their sum $(0, 1, 1)$ lies in $U_3$, so subtract it.

feedback.correct: Right. The pairwise test fails for three subspaces.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Try to write $\mathbf{0}$ with a non-zero piece from each subspace.

byKey.pairs: You applied the two-subspace test to three. Pairwise zero intersections do not stop $\mathbf{0}$ having a second representation.

explain.text: $(0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) = (0, 1, 1)$, which is in $U_3$. So $(0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) + (0, -1, -1) = \mathbf{0}$ with no zero piece. The sum is not direct.

screens.title: The third piece
screens.prose: We have $(0, 1, 0) \in U_1$ and $(0, 0, 1) \in U_2$. A third piece $\mathbf{u}_3 \in U_3$ closes the chain back to the origin. The dimensions, $2 + 1 + 1 = 4$, exceed 3. Lesson 4 shows why that rules out a direct sum.
screens.question: Find $\mathbf{u}_3$ with $(0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) + \mathbf{u}_3 = \mathbf{0}$.

hints.text: $\mathbf{u}_3$ undoes the first two pieces.
The first two add to $(0, 1, 1)$.
$\mathbf{u}_3 = -(0, 1, 1) = (0, -1, -1)$, which has the form $(0, y, y)$.

feedback.correct: Right. $(0, -1, -1) = (0, y, y)$ with $y = -1$, so it is in $U_3$.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the first two pieces and take the negative.

byKey.pos: You gave the sum of the first two pieces. $\mathbf{u}_3$ must cancel it, so flip the signs.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 3, one per coordinate.

explain.text: $(0, 1, 0) + (0, 0, 1) = (0, 1, 1)$, so $\mathbf{u}_3 = (0, -1, -1)$. It has the form $(0, y, y)$, so it lies in $U_3$. Three non-zero pieces add to $\mathbf{0}$.

screens.title: Even plus odd
screens.prose: In $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}}$, even functions ($f(-x) = f(x)$) and odd ones ($f(-x) = -f(x)$) form subspaces $U_e$ and $U_o$, and $\mathbb{R}^{\mathbb{R}} = U_e \oplus U_o$. Write $e^x = f_e(x) + f_o(x)$. Then $e^{-x} = f_e(x) - f_o(x)$.
screens.question: What is the even part $f_e(x)$ of $e^x$?

hints.text: Add the two equations.
$f_e(x) = \dfrac{e^x + e^{-x}}{2}$, which is $\cosh x$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add $e^x = f_e + f_o$ and $e^{-x} = f_e - f_o$.

byKey.odd: You subtracted the equations, which gives the odd part $\sinh x$.

explain.text: Adding gives $2f_e(x) = e^x + e^{-x}$, so $f_e = \cosh x$; subtracting gives $f_o = \sinh x$. Only the zero function is both even and odd. So the split is unique, and the sum is direct.

screens.title: Market and spread
screens.prose: One asset's returns over three days are $\mathbf{r} = (0.03, -0.01, 0.01)$, drawn in percent. Market moves are $U = \operatorname{span}\{(1, 1, 1)\}$; zero-sum moves are $W = \{x_1 + x_2 + x_3 = 0\}$. Then $\mathbb{R}^3 = U \oplus W$.
screens.question: Write $\mathbf{r} = \mathbf{m} + \mathbf{z}$ with $\mathbf{m} \in U$, $\mathbf{z} \in W$. What is $\mathbf{m}$?

hints.text: $\mathbf{m} = (c, c, c)$, and $\mathbf{z}$ must have entries summing to 0.
Entries of $\mathbf{r}$ sum to $0.03$, and entries of $\mathbf{m}$ to $3c$.
$3c = 0.03$, so $c = 0.01$: the mean return.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take $\mathbf{m} = (c, c, c)$ and make $\mathbf{r} - \mathbf{m}$ sum to 0.

byKey.swap: That is the zero-sum part $\mathbf{z}$. The market part has three equal entries.
byKey.sum: You used the total $0.03$ as each entry. Divide it by the 3 days.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 3, one per coordinate.

explain.text: The entries of $\mathbf{z}$ sum to 0, so $3c = 0.03$ and $c = 0.01$, the mean. Then $\mathbf{z} = (0.02, -0.02, 0)$. The sum is direct, so "how much was market" has exactly one answer.

ideas: $U$ is a subspace when it contains $\mathbf{0}$ and is closed under addition and scalar multiplication. The other conditions come free from $V$.
$U_1 + \dots + U_m$ is direct when each vector is written in one way. That happens exactly when $\mathbf{0}$ is.
Two subspaces give a direct sum exactly when $U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}$. For three or more, pairwise checks are not enough.

quiz.prose: Let $U' = \{\mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x_1 + 2x_2 + 3x_3 = 4\}$, a plane parallel to $U$.
quiz.question: Which check of the subspace test fails first?

options.why: It fails too, since a sum gives $4 + 4 = 8$, but the zero check fails first.
You trusted the shape. A plane missing the origin is not a subspace.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Put $\mathbf{0}$ into the equation.

explain.text: Substituting $\mathbf{0}$ gives $0 \ne 4$. Sums give 8 and multiples give $4\lambda$, so those fail too. Only a right side of 0 survives all three.

quiz.prose: In the proof that $U \cap W = \{\mathbf{0}\}$ makes $U + W$ direct, line 2 says: $\mathbf{u} = -\mathbf{w}$, and $-\mathbf{w} \in W$.
quiz.question: Why is $-\mathbf{w} \in W$?

options.text: $W$ is closed under scalar multiplication, and $-\mathbf{w} = (-1)\mathbf{w}$

options.why: Addition alone never produces $-\mathbf{w}$ from $\mathbf{w}$. Scaling by $-1$ does.
That is the hypothesis, used on the next line. It says nothing about $-\mathbf{w}$.

feedback.correct: Right. $(-1)\mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{w}$, and $W$ is closed under scaling.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write $-\mathbf{w}$ as a scalar times $\mathbf{w}$.

explain.text: Lesson 1 proved $(-1)\mathbf{w} = -\mathbf{w}$. A subspace is closed under scalar multiplication. So $-\mathbf{w}$ is in $W$.

quiz.prose: $U$ and $W$ are subspaces of $V$. The axes example showed that $U \cup W$ can fail to be a subspace.
quiz.question: When is $U \cup W$ a subspace?

options.text: Exactly when one of $U$, $W$ contains the other

options.why: The two axes are subspaces, and their union is not.
The axes meet only at $\mathbf{0}$, and their union fails. That condition is the test for a direct sum.
If $U \subseteq W$ then $U \cup W = W$, which is a subspace.

feedback.correct: Right. Otherwise a sum $\mathbf{u} + \mathbf{w}$ escapes both. The homework proves it.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Think of $U \subseteq W$, and of the two axes.

explain.text: If $U \subseteq W$, the union is $W$. If neither contains the other, take $\mathbf{u} \in U$ outside $W$ and $\mathbf{w} \in W$ outside $U$. Their sum lies in neither, as $(3, 2)$ did.

quiz.prose: The returns $\mathbf{r} = (0.03, -0.01, 0.01)$ split as $\mathbf{m} + \mathbf{z}$, with market part $\mathbf{m} = (0.01, 0.01, 0.01)$.
quiz.question: What is the zero-sum part $\mathbf{z}$?

feedback.correct: Right. $\mathbf{z} = \mathbf{r} - \mathbf{m} = (0.02, -0.02, 0)$, and its entries sum to 0.

byKey.add: You added $\mathbf{m}$ to $\mathbf{r}$. Subtract it instead.
byKey.length: Your answer has the wrong number of entries. It needs 3, one per coordinate.

explain.text: $\mathbf{z} = (0.03 - 0.01, -0.01 - 0.01, 0.01 - 0.01) = (0.02, -0.02, 0)$. Its entries sum to 0, so it lies in $W$. It is the move left after the market move.
